WA-2025-HB2681.title: Modifying cannabis producer, processor, and retailer license fees.
WA-2025-HB2681.summary:
The annual fees for cannabis producer, processor, and retail licenses are increased from $1,381 to $1,781.

Beginning July 1, 2027, the Liquor and Cannabis Board must add to the annual fee for issuance and renewal of the cannabis producer, processor, and retailer licenses the change in the Consumer Price Index since July 1, 2026. For purposes of the requirement, the Consumer Price Index means the Consumer Price Index for all urban consumers, all items, for the Seattle area as published by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics.

WA-2025-HB1916.title: Amending voter registration challenges and managing voter registration lists.
WA-2025-HB1916.summary:
Challenges to a Voter's Registration. Types of evidence that can be used to challenge a voter's registration are limited. A challenger may no longer base their challenge on the following:
• a search of county auditor records to determine whether the voter owns any property in the county;
• a search of local telephone directories to determine whether the voter maintains a telephone listing at any address in the county;
• a search of the voter registration database to determine whether the voter is registered at another address in the state; or
• a search of the voter registration database of another state to determine if the voter is registered in a state other than Washington.

If the challenger's proof is that the challenger sent a letter with return service to the challenged voter's address, the letter must be certified and sent using a form provided by the Office of the Secretary of State outlining the reason for the challenge.

Challengers must file a separate voter registration challenge form and signed affidavit for each voter whose registration is being challenged. Each form must include certain information, including a statement of the factual basis for the challenge and be signed under penalty of perjury. Each affidavit must be signed by hand with ink.

The timelines for which a county auditor publishes and removes information about a voter challenge from the auditor's website are amended.

Voter Challenge Proceedings . It is mandatory, rather than permissive, that a county auditor dismiss a challenge if the challenge is not in proper form or the factual basis does not meet the legal grounds for a challenge.

Before notifying the voter of a challenge, a county auditor may conduct an initial review of the merits of the challenge. If the county auditor determines that the challenge lacks merit by a preponderance of the evidence, then the county auditor may dismiss the challenge. A county auditor must attempt to reconfirm registration before scheduling a hearing. A hearing may only be scheduled if the county auditor is unable to confirm the voter's eligibility and there is probable cause that the challenged voter is not eligible to vote. If a county auditor independently verifies a voter's eligibility at any point, the county auditor may dismiss a challenge.

In addition to the county auditor, an auditor's designee is permitted to preside over the hearing. If the challenger does not attend the hearing in person, the challenge is dismissed. The challenged voter may appear in person or submit an affidavit. The challenger must prove that the registration is improper beyond a reasonable doubt, rather than by clear and convincing evidence. The notice to the challenged voter of the challenge and the scheduled hearing must provide additional information, including methods to confirm eligibility. Processes for successful voter registration challenges are provided.

WA-2025-HB1295.title: Using evidence-based instructional practices in reading and writing literacy for public elementary students.
WA-2025-HB1295.summary:
Literacy Curriculum Requirements . Beginning September 1, 2027, when a school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school updates or purchases a curriculum for early literacy, reading literacy, or writing literacy for use with any students in kindergarten through grade 4, the curriculum must include the following essential components: language comprehension, reading and writing fluency, orthographic knowledge, phonological awareness, vocabulary, and oral language development and proficiency.

The curriculum must also be:
• responsive to individual student needs, including by being multisensory, multimodal, high-quality, and culturally relevant;
• evidence-aligned to established interdisciplinary literacy research and evidence-informed in its instructional design;
• aligned with the state English Language Arts learning standards; and
• consistent with teacher endorsement standards for literacy-related competencies.

Unless it creates undue financial or operational burden, a school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school must implement the curriculum consistent with the developer's guidance and local policies, with the expectation of achieving full fidelity over time.

Teacher Literacy Endorsement Standards and Instructional Materials . Standards for teacher endorsements with literacy-related competencies must include the competencies needed to teach using a literacy curriculum that meets state requirements. Endorsements with literacy-related competencies include elementary education, ELA, literacy, special education, and any other endorsement determined by the Professional Educator Standards Board to include literacy-related competencies. The PESB must revise standards for endorsements with literacy-related competencies that do not meet state requirements.

The PESB must require approved teacher preparation programs to incorporate revised endorsement standards into their instructional content within two years after the year

of revision.

Within existing resources, the PESB must convene an advisory group to develop, review, and share instructional materials and open educational resources tailored to each endorsement and designed to prepare teacher candidates to use a literacy curriculum that meets state requirements.

Educator Literacy Training and Technical Assistance . The Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) must expand within available resources and in consultation with specified experts, the educator training program on dyslexia to apply to all students in kindergarten through grade 4. The program must be periodically updated.

Reporting by the educational service districts (ESDs) to the OSPI, and by the OSPI to the Legislature, on participation in the program is changed to biennial reporting, with the next report due in 2030.

WA-2025-HB2384.title: Increasing regulatory oversight of continuing care retirement communities.
WA-2025-HB2384.summary:
A new requirement is added to the application standards for registration as a continuing care retirement community (CCRC). Beginning July 1, 2027, if an applicant for registration as a CCRC offers life care contracts, it must provide an actuarial analysis to the Department of Social and Health Services (Department). A "life care contract" refers to a contract between a CCRC and a person to whom the CCRC agrees to provide lodging and any combination of nursing, medical, or personal care services for at least one year and up to the entirety of the person’s life. The contract is conditioned on payment of an entrance fee in lieu of, or in addition to, other recurring charges that do not change based on the care setting or services.

The actuarial analysis requirement begins with the applicant's second registration renewal and applies to every other subsequent registration renewal application. The actuarial analysis must have been prepared by a qualified actuary and include an actuarial memorandum and certification. Upon receipt of an actuarial analysis in application materials, the Department must transmit it to the Office of the Insurance Commissioner (Office) for review. The Department must adopt standards for the contents of the actuarial analysis materials to be submitted. The Office must adopt standards for the review of the actuarial analyses, the qualifications of the actuaries preparing the analyses, and the administration of appeals of determinations that an applicant's actuarial balance is not satisfactory.

The Office's standards must include a process for determining the applicant's ability to meet its overall contract obligations under its life care contracts in accordance with actuarial standards of practice. The standards must consider whether the applicant's actuarial balance is satisfactory and reflects liabilities that are sufficient to cover obligations under moderately adverse conditions during the testing period. The term "moderately adverse conditions" is defined as anticipating unfavorable, but not extreme, events with a reasonable probability of occurring during the testing period.

Upon concluding its review, the Office must determine whether the applicant's actuarial balance is satisfactory under the review standards and notify the Department and the applicant of the results. If the Office's review finds that the applicant has not satisfied the review requirement, it will notify the applicant of its right to appeal the decision to the Office and provide the reasons for the determination to allow the applicant to attempt to cure the deficiencies.

For those CCRC applicants required to submit an actuarial analysis, the Department's decision to issue a registration depends on the receipt of a notice of completion of the actuarial analysis review from the Office. WA-2025-HB2296.title: Expanding the use of distributed energy resources.
WA-2025-HB2296.summary:
Meter-Mounted Devices .

Authorization for Use.

All electric utilities must allow their customers to have one meter-mounted device between the customer's meter and the meter socket if certain installation and device requirements are met. Meter-mounted devices are owned by the customer.

Installation Requirements .

Meter-mounted device installation must follow the National Electrical Code, be done by a licensed electrical contractor, and be approved by the local permitting authority. Once a customer identifies a licensed electrical contractor, the customer must work with the utility to find a mutually agreeable time for a utility representative to inspect and approve the meter for use with the meter-mounted device, and then to remove and then reconnect the utility's meter so the contractor can install the device.

Device Specifications .

A meter-mounted device must be:
• qualified to connect to the supply side of the service disconnect per the National Electric Code;
• approved or listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory and certified to meet all applicable standards as determined by such a laboratory;
• suitable for use in 200 amperes meter sockets;
• compatible with advanced metering infrastructure; and
• approved by the utility.

A meter-mounted device must not:
• impede access to specified parts of the meter or switchboard or otherwise interfere with maintenance and testing; or
• interfere with meter functions or communication networks.

Manufacturer Request and Utility Device Approval Process.

After receiving a request from a manufacturer for the approval of a specific meter-mounted device model, an electric utility must decide on whether to approve or disapprove the device based on whether the device meets the device specifications. After receiving such a request, a utility with more than 25,000 customers must make an approval decision within 90 days, and a utility with 25,000 customers or fewer must make a decision within 180 days. The utility must post its approval decisions on its website.

Utility Cost Recovery .

Utilities may charge customers to recover the service costs of work on a meter-mounted device, or maintenance or repair work on utility equipment necessary to the device's installation.

Implementation Timeline.

Utilities must implement these meter-mounted device policies by 6 months of the effective date of this act.

Utility Liabilit y.

Utilities may not be liable for damage to any person or property from a meter-mounted device.

Utility Removal Authorization.

Utilities may have a qualified utility employee, or a licensed electrical contractor remove a meter-mounted device that inhibits the utility's ability to provide service or read the meter, or that does not meet the required device specifications.

Restriction on Local Jurisdictions.

Cities, counties, or other local jurisdictions may not prohibit the installation and operation of a meter-mounted device.

WA-2025-HB2274.title: Modifying the Washington commercial electronic mail act.
WA-2025-HB2274.summary:
In order for a commercial email subject line to be considered false or misleading under the CEMA, the person must have actual knowledge or knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances that the subject line contains false or misleading information.

Statutory damages for a recipient of a prohibited commercial email or commercial text message are lowered to $100, or actual damages, whichever is greater.

All causes of action commenced on or after the effective date of the act are subject to these provisions, regardless of when the conduct occurred.

WA-2025-SB5690.title: Concerning utility relocation.
WA-2025-SB5690.summary:
WSDOT is directed to adopt and maintain agency policies that:
• proactively provide utility owners with information about planned state highway fish barrier removal projects to enable collaboration between utility owners and WSDOT, with at least one year of advance notice whenever feasible; and
• maximize the amount of federal funding for fish barrier removal projects that also allow the funds to be used for utility relocation costs by WSDOT or utilities under federal rules and regulations.

WSDOT is encouraged to:
• ensure that if utility relocation costs are an eligible use under federal rules and regulations, any awards received are deposited into the Multimodal Transportation Account; and
• report to the Legislature and Office of Financial Management any recommendations for changes to state law, rules, or policies that would allow WSDOT or utilities to more efficiently receive competitive federal grant funding or reimbursements for utility relocation to the extent permitted by the terms of federal programs and applicable federal regulations.

WA-2025-SB5915.title: Concerning the health technology assessment program.
WA-2025-SB5915.summary:
In selecting health technologies to be reviewed under the Health Technology Assessment Program, the Health Care Authority (Authority) must give priority to an additional category of health technologies. The new priority category relates to health technologies that have patient access established or recommended for a patient population under Medicare or in nationally recognized expert treatment guidelines, including guidelines adopted by specialty physician organizations or patient advocacy organizations.

When the health technology pertains to a life-threatening or rare disease, the Health Technology Clinical Committee (Committee) must:
• evaluate all applicable clinical trials regarding the technology, as published in peer-reviewed clinical literature, including randomized control trials; and
• consider information submitted by clinical experts indicating that a randomized control trial or other specific trial design would be unethical, impractical, or impossible for the technology within a specific patient population.

Re-reviews of health technologies are not limited to evidence made available since the previous determination. Re-reviews must consider new evidence in combination with, and within the context of, the clinical evidence the Committee had previously considered.

The Authority must publish on its website the receipt of submissions for new technology assessments and re-review assessments with 30 days of receipt. The Committee must review the submissions and communicate its decision to review or re-review within 180 days. If the Committee issues an adverse determination, it must provide the submitting party with a written, substantive explanation of the rationale for the adverse determination within 180 days from the date of submission.

WA-2025-SB6031.title: Enhancing public safety and enforcement of crimes that impact insurance.
WA-2025-SB6031.summary:
Insurance Fraud Program .

The personnel that the Commissioner may employ must be qualified by training and experience in the areas of detection, investigation, or prosecution of fraud and other other crimes in which the insurance industry or an insurance consumer or beneficiary is a victim or impacted, instead of qualified by training and experience in the areas of detection, investigation, or prosecution of fraud in which the insurance industry is a victim.

Insurance Fraud Program—Purpose .

The Program's purpose is revised to make a purpose to confront the problem of insurance fraud and other crimes that impact the insurance industry, or insurance consumers or beneficiaries in Washington, by updating definitions to address recurring or technologically sophisticated fraud schemes, and making a concerted effort to: detect such crimes, reduce their occurrence through criminal enforcement and deterrence; require restitution of expenses incurred by an insurer in investigating or paying fraudulent claims or resulting from other crimes; and require restitution to insurance consumers victimized by insurance fraud and other insurance-related crimes. The primary focus of the insurance fraud program is revised to be not only on organized fraudulent activities committed against insurance companies, but also organized or collusive criminal schemes that impact insurance companies or insurance consumers.

Insurance Fraud Program—Definitions and Crime of Insurance Fraud .

The definition of "insurance fraud" in the Program is revised and restructured as a crime of Insurance Fraud, punishable as a class B felony. Willful embezzlement, abstracting, purloining, or conversion of moneys, funds, premiums, credits, or other property of an insurer or person engaged in the business of insurance is changed to embezzling, abstracting, purloining, or engaging or conspiring in conversion of moneys, funds, premiums, credits, benefits, or other property of an insurer or person engaged in the business of insurance, or insurance consumer or beneficiary.

Insurance Fraud also includes submitting a bill or claim to an insurer or insurance consumer:
• for medical, vehicle, or property services not rendered, vehicle or property repairs not made, or supplies not provided;
• using a current procedural terminology code or health care common procedure coding system code not reasonably appropriate to the service provided or procedure performed; or
• using the name, credentials, or national provider identifier of a health care provider who neither rendered nor supervised the billed service.

Insurance Fraud also includes:
• submitting a statement, estimate, invoice, bid, proposal, proof of loss, or any other document that misrepresents the scope of damages or costs of repairs associated with a property insurance claim;
• falsifying diagnostic or treatment information in a patient's medical file to bill for treatments or prescriptions that would not otherwise have been covered by the…
